Southeast Asia.0: Southeast Asia was home to Hoabinhian hunter-gatherers who foraged forests, rivers and coasts with stone tools. As the Ice Age ended, rising seas drowned the land bridge called Sundaland, creating today's islands and coastlines. Late in this era, the first farmers from southern China began edging toward the region.
Southeast Asia.1: Austronesian-speaking peoples began expanding from Taiwan c. 3000 BC, sailing outrigger canoes south toward the Philippines and carrying pottery, pigs and rice. On the mainland, Neolithic farmers from southern China settled river valleys, growing rice and millet in villages such as Ban Kao in Thailand and Phung Nguyen in Vietnam.
Southeast Asia.2: Austronesian seafarers spread through the Philippines, Borneo, Sulawesi and the Indonesian islands, mixing with older populations, and some pushed into the open Pacific. On the mainland, farming villages multiplied and bronze working appeared c. 1500 to 1000 BC at sites such as Ban Chiang in Thailand, slowly enriching local elites.
Southeast Asia.3: The Dong Son bronze culture flourished in the Red River valley of northern Vietnam, famous for great decorated bronze drums. Later Vietnamese tradition places the Van Lang kingdom of the Hung kings here. Across the region, wet-rice farming villages grew larger and chiefs gained power by controlling metal, land and trade.
Southeast Asia.4: Dong Son chiefdoms in northern Vietnam kept producing bronze drums that were traded far into the islands, while the Sa Huynh culture of central Vietnam buried its dead in large jars. Iron tools were beginning to spread, helping farmers clear land, and sea trade routes slowly linked the coasts together.
Southeast Asia.5: Iron working spread across mainland Southeast Asia, strengthening farming and warfare among chiefdoms. Sa Huynh traders exchanged distinctive jade and glass ornaments across the South China Sea with the Philippines, Borneo and Taiwan. Dong Son drums circulated across the archipelago as prized symbols of rank and wealth.
Southeast Asia.6: Iron Age chiefdoms ruled villages across the mainland and islands, and trade quickened. Ports on the Thai-Malay peninsula such as Khao Sam Kaeo began exchanging goods with merchants from India, an early sign of the Indian influence that would later shape religion, writing and kingship across the region.
Southeast Asia.7: In northern Vietnam, tradition credits An Duong Vuong with founding the kingdom of Au Lac c. 257 BC, centered on the spiral citadel of Co Loa. Late in the century, the Chinese general Zhao Tuo founded Nanyue in the south of China. In Burma, early Pyu walled towns were beginning to appear.
Southeast Asia.8: Nanyue absorbed Au Lac early in the century, and in 111 BC Han China conquered Nanyue and northern Vietnam, beginning about a thousand years of Chinese rule. Elsewhere, Pyu city-states grew in Burma, and maritime trade increasingly linked India, Southeast Asian ports and China.
Southeast Asia.9: Northern Vietnam was governed as the Han province of Jiaozhi, where Chinese officials, taxes and customs pressed on local Viet lords. Further south and west, Pyu towns, Mekong delta settlements and island chiefdoms grew rich on the sea trade carrying beads, spices and metals between India and China.
Southeast Asia.10: In AD 40 the Trung Sisters led a revolt against Han rule in northern Vietnam, but Chinese general Ma Yuan crushed it by 43, tightening Chinese control. In the Mekong delta, the kingdom later known as Funan began to emerge, trading with India and adopting Indian ideas about kingship.
Southeast Asia.11: Funan grew into the region's first great trading state, with its port of Oc Eo handling goods from India, China and even Rome. In 192 the Cham founded a kingdom on the central Vietnamese coast, later called Champa. Indian religions, Sanskrit and political ideas were steadily taking root.
Southeast Asia.12: Funan reached a peak under rulers such as Fan Shiman, controlling trade across the Gulf of Thailand, and Chinese envoys visited c. 245 and wrote the first detailed accounts. In northern Vietnam, Lady Trieu led a famous revolt against Chinese rule in 248. Champa and the Pyu cities continued to grow.
Southeast Asia.13: Funan, Champa and the Pyu cities flourished as Indian-influenced kingdoms whose rulers used Sanskrit titles and patronized Hindu and Buddhist cults. Northern Vietnam remained under Chinese dynasties. Late in the century, kings in eastern Borneo began carving Sanskrit inscriptions, the oldest known writing in the Indonesian islands.
Southeast Asia.14: Sanskrit inscriptions record kings at Kutai in Borneo and Tarumanagara in western Java, showing Indian-style kingship spreading through the islands. Funan and Champa remained major coastal powers, and Buddhism grew among merchants and courts. Northern Vietnam stayed a Chinese province ruled by southern Chinese dynasties.
Southeast Asia.15: Funan declined and the Khmer kingdom of Chenla rose in its place along the Mekong. The Mon people built the Buddhist Dvaravati culture in central Thailand. In northern Vietnam, Ly Bi briefly declared an independent state in 544, though Chinese rule returned by 602.
Southeast Asia.16: Srivijaya, based at Palembang in Sumatra, rose c. 670 to control the Strait of Malacca and the sea trade between India and China. It became a famous Buddhist center visited by the Chinese pilgrim Yijing. On the mainland, Khmer Chenla, Mon Dvaravati and Champa thrived, while Tang China ruled northern Vietnam as Annam.
Southeast Asia.17: The Buddhist Sailendra dynasty rose in central Java, rivaling Hindu kings and launching sea raids on Champa and Chenla. Chenla split into rival halves, while Srivijaya kept its grip on the straits. Late in the century, work began in Java on the vast Buddhist monument of Borobudur.
Southeast Asia.18: Borobudur was completed in Java c. 800, followed by the Hindu temples of Prambanan. In 802 Jayavarman II proclaimed himself universal king and founded the Khmer Empire in Cambodia. In Burma, raids from Nanzhao weakened the Pyu cities, and Bamar people settled the dry zone around Pagan.
Southeast Asia.19: In 938 Ngo Quyen defeated Chinese fleets at the Bach Dang River, winning Vietnam's independence after about a thousand years of Chinese rule; by 968 it was the kingdom of Dai Co Viet. The Khmer built grand temples around Angkor, and Javanese power shifted from central to eastern Java.
Southeast Asia.20: King Anawrahta unified Burma from Pagan and championed Theravada Buddhism. Vietnam's Ly dynasty moved the capital to Thang Long, today's Hanoi, in 1010. The Indian Chola empire raided Srivijaya in 1025, weakening it, while Airlangga rebuilt a strong kingdom in eastern Java and the Khmer expanded under Suryavarman I.
Southeast Asia.21: The Khmer Empire peaked as Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat c. 1113 to 1150, the world's largest religious monument. Pagan's kings filled the Burmese plain with thousands of temples. After a Cham army sacked Angkor in 1177, Jayavarman VII drove them out and began rebuilding his capital on a grand scale.
Southeast Asia.22: The Mongols invaded Vietnam, Burma and Java, but were largely repelled; Tran Hung Dao's victories in Vietnam became legendary, though Pagan's kingdom collapsed after 1287. Thai peoples founded Sukhothai c. 1238 as Khmer power waned. In northern Sumatra, Samudra Pasai became one of the first Muslim kingdoms in the region.
Southeast Asia.23: Majapahit, founded in Java in 1293, came to dominate much of the archipelago under its minister Gajah Mada. On the mainland, Thai kings founded Ayutthaya in 1351 and the Lao kingdom of Lan Xang arose in 1353, both pressing on a weakening Khmer Empire. Dai Viet fought long wars with Champa.
Southeast Asia.24: Malacca rose c. 1400 as the region's great port, and its rulers' conversion helped Islam spread along trade routes. Siam sacked Angkor in 1431, and the Khmer moved their capital south. Ming China briefly occupied Vietnam from 1407 to 1427 before the Le dynasty restored independence and later crushed Champa in 1471.
Southeast Asia.25: Portugal seized Malacca in 1511, and Magellan's fleet reached the Philippines in 1521; from 1565 Spain colonized the islands from Manila. Majapahit faded as Muslim sultanates such as Demak, Aceh and Johor rose. In Burma, the Toungoo king Bayinnaung built a huge empire and conquered Ayutthaya, which regained freedom under Naresuan.
Southeast Asia.26: The Dutch East India Company founded Batavia in 1619, took Malacca in 1641 and gradually seized control of the spice trade. Sultan Agung's Mataram dominated Java, while Spanish galleons linked Manila to Mexico. Vietnam was split between rival Trinh and Nguyen lords, and Ayutthaya traded and sparred with Europeans under King Narai.
Southeast Asia.27: The Dutch East India Company deepened its control of Java by meddling in Mataram's succession wars, and in 1740 its forces massacred Chinese residents of Batavia. The southern Nguyen lords pushed Vietnamese settlement into the Mekong delta. Ayutthaya enjoyed a prosperous last golden age, while Burma's Toungoo dynasty declined.
Southeast Asia.28: Burma revived under the Konbaung dynasty and sacked Ayutthaya in 1767. Taksin rallied the Siamese, and in 1782 Rama I founded the Chakri dynasty with a new capital at Bangkok. The Tay Son rebellion overturned Vietnam's ruling houses, Britain took Penang in 1786, and the bankrupt Dutch company dissolved in 1799.
Southeast Asia.29: In 1802 Gia Long founded the Nguyen dynasty and unified Vietnam. Britain briefly ruled Java under Raffles, then founded Singapore in 1819 as a free port. The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 divided the Malay world into British and Dutch spheres, and the First Anglo-Burmese War began that same year.
Southeast Asia.30: Burma lost coastal provinces to Britain in 1826, and Britain grouped Penang, Malacca and Singapore as the Straits Settlements. In Java, Prince Diponegoro's revolt of 1825 to 1830 was crushed, and the Dutch imposed the Cultivation System, forcing peasants to grow export crops. Siam and Vietnam vied for control of Cambodia.
Southeast Asia.31: France invaded Vietnam in 1858, took Cochinchina in 1862 and made Cambodia a protectorate in 1863. Britain annexed Lower Burma in 1852. Siam's King Mongkut signed trade treaties to keep Europeans at bay, and in 1873 the Dutch began a long, brutal war to conquer Aceh in Sumatra.
Southeast Asia.32: France formed French Indochina in 1887 and added Laos in 1893, while Britain conquered all of Burma by 1885. Siam stayed independent as a buffer under the reforming King Chulalongkorn. Filipinos rose against Spain in 1896, but in 1898 the United States took the Philippines and soon fought a bloody war there.
Southeast Asia.33: The Philippine-American War left the US firmly in control, and the Dutch completed their conquest of Aceh, shaping the borders of modern Indonesia. Siam ceded border lands to France and Britain to keep its independence. Rubber and tin booms reshaped colonies, and early nationalist groups such as Budi Utomo appeared in Java.
Southeast Asia.34: Colonial economies boomed on rubber, tin, oil and rice exports, drawing in Chinese and Indian migrants. In the Dutch East Indies, Sarekat Islam became the first mass nationalist movement. Siam joined the Allies in World War I in 1917, and Vietnamese patriots such as Phan Boi Chau sought ways to end French rule.
Southeast Asia.35: Nationalism and communism spread among educated young people. Communists in the Dutch East Indies rose in revolt in 1926 to 1927 and were crushed, while Sukarno founded the Indonesian Nationalist Party in 1927. Ho Chi Minh organized Vietnamese revolutionaries from abroad, and colonial powers met dissent with arrests and exile.
Southeast Asia.36: The Great Depression hit export economies hard, sparking unrest such as the Yen Bai mutiny and the founding of the Indochinese Communist Party in 1930. A 1932 revolution made Siam a constitutional monarchy, renamed Thailand in 1939. The Philippines became a self-governing commonwealth in 1935, and Burma was separated from British India.
Southeast Asia.37: Japan occupied nearly all of Southeast Asia from 1942 to 1945, toppling European colonial rule. After the war, Vietnam, Indonesia, the Philippines and Burma declared or won independence, though Indonesians fought the Dutch until 1949 and the Vietnamese began a war against France. In Malaya, a communist insurgency began in 1948.
Southeast Asia.38: France was defeated at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, and the Geneva conference split Vietnam into a communist north and a US-backed south; Laos and Cambodia were already independent. Malaya gained independence in 1957. Indonesia hosted the 1955 Bandung Conference of newly free nations, and Sukarno moved toward authoritarian 'Guided Democracy'.
Southeast Asia.39: The US fought in the Vietnam War from 1965 to 1973, bombing heavily across Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia. In Indonesia, an alleged coup attempt led to mass killings of suspected communists in 1965 to 1966 and Suharto's rise. Malaysia formed in 1963, Singapore separated in 1965, and ASEAN was founded in 1967.
Southeast Asia.40: Saigon fell in 1975 and Vietnam was unified under communist rule, while Laos also became communist. In Cambodia, the Khmer Rouge genocide of 1975 to 1979 killed about 1.5 to 2 million people until Vietnam invaded. Indonesia occupied East Timor, Marcos ruled the Philippines under martial law, and refugees fled by sea.
Southeast Asia.41: Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 opened its economy, while its army occupied Cambodia. People Power protests toppled Marcos in the Philippines in 1986, and a 1988 uprising in Burma was crushed by the army. Singapore, Thailand and Malaysia grew rapidly, and Brunei became independent in 1984.
Southeast Asia.42: Cambodia's war ended with the 1991 Paris accords and UN-run elections in 1993. ASEAN expanded to include Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and Cambodia. The 1997 Asian financial crisis devastated economies and helped topple Suharto in 1998, opening Indonesia to democracy, and East Timor voted for independence in 1999 amid violence.
Southeast Asia.43: Timor-Leste became independent in 2002, and Indonesia consolidated democracy, making peace in Aceh in 2005. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed about 230,000 people around the ocean, many in Aceh and Thailand. Terrorist bombings struck Bali, Thailand's army staged a coup in 2006, and Cyclone Nargis devastated Myanmar in 2008.
Southeast Asia.44: Myanmar's military loosened its grip, and Aung San Suu Kyi's party won elections in 2015, yet the army drove over 700,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh in 2017. Thailand's army seized power again in 2014. Disputes with China over the South China Sea sharpened, while Vietnam, Indonesia and the Philippines grew fast.
Southeast Asia.45: Myanmar's military seized power in a 2021 coup, sparking a widespread civil war. The region recovered from COVID-19 and courted trade shifting away from China, while South China Sea tensions persisted. Ferdinand Marcos Jr. won the Philippine presidency in 2022, Prabowo took office in Indonesia in 2024, and Timor-Leste joined ASEAN in 2025.

Japan.0: People reached the Japanese islands at least 38,000 years ago, and from c. 14,000 BC the Jōmon culture made some of the world's oldest pottery. Jōmon people hunted deer, fished and gathered nuts, and as the climate warmed and seas rose, they settled into lasting villages of pit houses.
Japan.1: The Middle Jōmon period was the high point of this hunter-gatherer culture, with the largest population and big villages such as Sannai-Maruyama in northern Honshu. People made dramatic flame-style pottery and clay dogū figurines, managed chestnut groves and traded obsidian and jade over long distances.
Japan.2: In the Late Jōmon period, a cooler climate reduced food supplies and populations fell, especially in the east. Communities built ritual stone circles such as those at Ōyu and made elaborate dogū figures. People still lived mainly by hunting, fishing and gathering, perhaps with some small-scale plant growing.
Japan.3: Migrants from the Korean peninsula brought wet-rice farming to northern Kyushu, starting the Yayoi culture c. 900 to 300 BC, though dates are debated. Elsewhere Jōmon life continued. Later Japanese chronicles placed the legendary founding by Emperor Jimmu in 660 BC, a date historians treat as myth.
Japan.4: Yayoi rice farming spread slowly eastward from Kyushu into western Honshu, carried by newcomers and adopted by Jōmon descendants. Farmers dug irrigated paddies and stored grain, which allowed larger villages. Most of eastern and northern Japan still lived the older Jōmon way.
Japan.5: The Yayoi farming way of life kept spreading across western Japan, bringing new tools, woven cloth and continental-style pottery. Villages began building moats and fences for defense, a sign of growing competition over land and harvests. Bronze and iron objects arrived from the continent through Korea.
Japan.6: Yayoi farming communities grew larger and more unequal, with leaders buried in richer graves. Iron tools and bronze bells, swords and mirrors, first imported and then made locally, became symbols of power. In Hokkaido, people continued a hunting and fishing culture descended from the Jōmon.
Japan.7: Yayoi villages formed small chiefdoms, some ringed with deep moats like the growing settlement at Yoshinogari in Kyushu. Warfare between communities appears in weapons and injured skeletons. Rice farming had reached much of Honshu, while the north kept older lifeways that later fed into Ainu culture.
Japan.8: Chinese records describe the people of Wa, or Japan, as divided into more than a hundred small countries, some sending envoys to Han China's new commanderies in Korea after 108 BC. Chiefs prized Chinese bronze mirrors and iron, and rivalry among Yayoi chiefdoms was intensifying.
Japan.9: Wa chiefdoms in Kyushu traded with the Han outpost of Lelang in Korea, gaining mirrors, iron and prestige goods. Rice farming supported growing populations, and local rulers used bronze ritual objects to display power. Japan remained a patchwork of competing Yayoi polities.
Japan.10: In AD 57 the king of Na, a small Wa state in Kyushu, sent envoys to Han China and received a gold seal from Emperor Guangwu, a seal later found in 1784. Yayoi chiefdoms were consolidating into larger regional powers, competing for iron and continental contacts.
Japan.11: A Wa king sent envoys to Han China in 107, but late in the century Chinese sources describe the Wa lands falling into prolonged warfare. Larger confederations were forming, and leaders built bigger burial mounds. These conflicts set the stage for a ruling queen who would unite many states.
Japan.12: Queen Himiko of Yamatai, a ruler said to use spiritual powers, led a league of some 30 Wa states and sent envoys to the Chinese state of Wei in 239. After her death c. 248, the first huge keyhole-shaped tombs appeared, marking the start of the Kofun period.
Japan.13: In the Kofun period, the Yamato kings in the Nara basin built massive keyhole-shaped tombs and extended alliances across western Japan. Iron from the Korean peninsula was vital to their power, and Yamato forces were involved in peninsular wars, as a Goguryeo stele records from 391 onward.
Japan.14: Yamato power peaked with gigantic tombs such as the Daisen Kofun near Osaka, attributed to Emperor Nintoku. The 'five kings of Wa' sent envoys to China's Southern dynasties seeking titles. Immigrants from Korea brought writing, crafts and administrative skills, and society was organized into hereditary clans called uji.
Japan.15: Buddhism arrived from the Korean kingdom of Baekje in 538 or 552, dividing the court. The pro-Buddhist Soga clan defeated the rival Mononobe in 587 and dominated the Yamato court. Empress Suiko took the throne in 593, opening the Asuka period with Prince Shōtoku as her regent.
Japan.16: Prince Shōtoku issued his Seventeen-Article Constitution in 604 and sent envoys to Sui China. The Taika reforms of 645 began building a Chinese-style centralized state. After defeat by Tang and Silla in Korea in 663, rulers strengthened defenses, and under Emperor Tenmu the names 'Nihon' and 'tennō' came into use.
Japan.17: The Taihō Code of 701 set up a Chinese-style legal state, and in 710 the court moved to a grand planned capital at Nara. The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki chronicles were written, and Emperor Shōmu built the Great Buddha at Tōdai-ji. In 794 the capital moved to Heian, today's Kyoto.
Japan.18: The Heian court flourished in Kyoto as the Fujiwara clan married daughters into the imperial family and ruled as regents. The monks Saichō and Kūkai founded the Tendai and Shingon schools of Buddhism. Japan ended embassies to Tang China in 894, and kana scripts began to develop.
Japan.19: The Fujiwara regents dominated an elegant court culture, celebrated in poetry collections such as the Kokinshū of 905. In the provinces, private estates grew and warrior bands formed, shown by Taira no Masakado's revolt in 939. Real power was slowly shifting from the court to armed landowners.
Japan.20: Fujiwara no Michinaga brought the regents' power to its height, and court ladies wrote classics such as The Tale of Genji c. 1010 and The Pillow Book. Warrior clans fought wars in the north for the court. From 1086, retired emperors began ruling from the cloister to counter the Fujiwara.
Japan.21: Warrior clans became kingmakers in court disputes, and Taira no Kiyomori briefly dominated the government. The Minamoto won the Genpei War in 1185, and in 1192 Minamoto no Yoritomo became the first shogun, ruling from Kamakura. Samurai rule had begun, and lasted nearly seven centuries.
Japan.22: After Yoritomo, the Hōjō family ruled as regents for the Kamakura shoguns and defeated the court in 1221. New popular Buddhist movements such as Pure Land, Zen and Nichiren spread. Mongol invasions in 1274 and 1281 were repelled, helped by storms later called kamikaze, though the defense strained the shogunate.
Japan.23: Emperor Go-Daigo overthrew the Kamakura shogunate in 1333, but Ashikaga Takauji soon set up a new shogunate in Kyoto. Rival Northern and Southern imperial courts fought until 1392. Under Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, culture blossomed with Noh theater and the Golden Pavilion.
Japan.24: The Ashikaga shoguns traded with Ming China and patronized Zen arts like the tea ceremony and ink painting. But the Ōnin War of 1467 to 1477 wrecked Kyoto and started the Sengoku, or warring states, era, as regional lords called daimyō fought for power. Ryukyu was unified in 1429.
Japan.25: The Portuguese brought guns in 1543 and Francis Xavier introduced Christianity in 1549. Oda Nobunaga began uniting the country with gunpowder armies, and Toyotomi Hideyoshi completed unification in 1590. Hideyoshi then invaded Korea in 1592 to 1598, a costly failure that ended with his death.
Japan.26: Tokugawa Ieyasu won at Sekigahara in 1600 and founded the Tokugawa shogunate in 1603, bringing over 250 years of peace. After the Christian-led Shimabara uprising, Japan closed itself to most foreigners in the 1630s, trading only with the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki. Cities like Edo and Osaka boomed.
Japan.27: Under the Tokugawa peace, Edo grew to about a million people, one of the largest cities in the world. Shogun Yoshimune's Kyōhō reforms tried to repair finances, and he eased the ban on Western books, encouraging 'Dutch learning'. Kabuki, puppet theater and woodblock prints thrived in the cities.
Japan.28: Merchants grew rich while many samurai fell into debt, and the official Tanuma Okitsugu promoted commerce. The Tenmei famine of the 1780s killed many and led to the strict Kansei reforms. Scholars translated Western anatomy books, while others revived study of ancient Japanese texts. Russian ships began appearing in the north.
Japan.29: The Tokugawa shogunate still ruled a stable, closed Japan, but foreign ships increasingly appeared, including Russian raids in the north and a British warship at Nagasaki in 1808. Ino Tadataka mapped the coastline. Urban culture flourished, with kabuki, popular novels and the early work of Hokusai.
Japan.30: The shogunate ordered foreign ships repelled in 1825. Famine in the 1830s sparked unrest, including Ōshio Heihachirō's 1837 uprising in Osaka, and the Tenpō reforms tried to restore order. Hokusai's Great Wave was printed c. 1831, and news of China's defeat in the Opium War alarmed Japan's leaders.
Japan.31: Commodore Perry forced Japan open in 1853, and unequal treaties followed. Anger at the weak shogunate led samurai from domains like Satsuma and Chōshū to topple it, and the 1868 Meiji Restoration returned power to the emperor. Japan abolished domains and samurai privileges and raced to modernize.
Japan.32: Meiji Japan built railways, factories, schools and a conscript army, crushing the samurai Satsuma Rebellion in 1877. It annexed Ryukyu as Okinawa in 1879 and adopted a constitution in 1889. In 1894 to 1895 Japan defeated China and took Taiwan, joining the imperial powers.
Japan.33: Japan allied with Britain in 1902 and defeated Russia in 1904 to 1905, the first modern Asian victory over a European power. It made Korea a protectorate and gained influence in Manchuria. Industry grew quickly, but heavy war costs and taxes caused unrest at home.
Japan.34: Japan annexed Korea in 1910. Emperor Meiji died in 1912, beginning the Taishō era. In World War I Japan seized German holdings in China and the Pacific and pressed its Twenty-One Demands on China. Wartime booms brought inflation, and rice riots erupted in 1918.
Japan.35: 'Taishō democracy' brought party governments and mass politics, and men gained universal suffrage in 1925, alongside a harsh law against radicals. The Great Kantō Earthquake of 1923 devastated Tokyo and Yokohama. Emperor Hirohito's Shōwa era began in 1926, and a financial panic struck in 1927.
Japan.36: The army seized Manchuria in 1931, and Japan left the League of Nations. Military officers gained control at home through assassinations and pressure on governments. In 1937 full-scale war with China began, including the Nanjing massacre, as Japan mobilized its whole economy for war.
Japan.37: Japan joined the Axis, attacked Pearl Harbor in 1941 and conquered much of Asia before being pushed back. After atomic bombs fell on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945, Japan surrendered and was occupied by the US, which oversaw land reform and a 1947 constitution renouncing war.
Japan.38: Japan regained sovereignty in 1952 under a security treaty with the US. Boosted by Korean War orders, its 'economic miracle' began, with fast-growing steel, shipbuilding and electronics. The Liberal Democratic Party formed in 1955 and would govern for most of the following decades.
Japan.39: Japan's economy grew around 10 percent a year, and by 1968 it was the world's second-largest. The 1964 Tokyo Olympics and the first bullet train showcased its recovery. Mass protests opposed the 1960 security treaty with the US, while pollution scandals revealed the costs of rapid growth.
Japan.40: Japan hosted the 1970 Osaka Expo, regained Okinawa from the US in 1972 and established relations with China. The 1973 oil shock ended the era of super-fast growth, but Japanese cars and electronics conquered world markets thanks to efficient manufacturing.
Japan.41: Japan's economy reached its peak, with booming exports and soaring land and stock prices after the 1985 Plaza Accord. Emperor Hirohito died in 1989, beginning the Heisei era. The asset bubble burst in 1989 to 1991, leaving banks with massive bad debts.
Japan.42: The 'Lost Decade' of stagnation followed the bubble, with falling prices and a banking crisis in 1997 to 1998. In 1995 the Kobe earthquake killed over 6,000 people, and the Aum Shinrikyō cult released sarin gas in the Tokyo subway. The LDP briefly lost power in 1993.
Japan.43: Prime Minister Koizumi pushed reforms and privatization from 2001 to 2006, but deflation persisted and the 2008 global crisis hit exports. Japan's population began to shrink and age rapidly. In 2009 voters ended the LDP's long rule by electing the Democratic Party of Japan.
Japan.44: The 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami killed about 18,000 people and caused the Fukushima nuclear disaster. Shinzō Abe returned as prime minister in 2012, pursuing 'Abenomics' and a stronger defense role. Emperor Akihito abdicated in 2019, and Naruhito's Reiwa era began.
Japan.45: Japan weathered COVID-19 and held the delayed Tokyo Olympics in 2021. Former prime minister Abe was assassinated in 2022. Facing China and North Korea, Japan sharply raised defense spending, and in 2025 Sanae Takaichi became its first female prime minister amid a weak yen and a shrinking population.

Korea.0: Humans lived on the Korean peninsula from the Old Stone Age, hunting and gathering. From c. 8000 BC people of the Jeulmun culture made some of the region's earliest pottery and lived by fishing, shellfish gathering and hunting along coasts and rivers, leaving behind large shell middens.
Korea.1: Jeulmun people, known for comb-patterned pottery, lived in small villages and had begun growing millet alongside fishing and gathering. Korean tradition holds that the mythical Dangun founded Gojoseon, the first Korean kingdom, in 2333 BC, though historians see this as legend rather than recorded history.
Korea.2: The Mumun pottery period began c. 1500 BC as new farming communities grew rice, millet and beans in larger villages. People built thousands of stone dolmen tombs, and Korea now holds a large share of the world's dolmens. Bronze objects began to appear late in this era.
Korea.3: Mumun farmers expanded rice paddies, and local elites displayed wealth through bronze daggers and dolmen burials, such as those at Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa. In the northwest and Liaodong, Gojoseon was emerging as a real chiefdom or early state linked to the bronze cultures of northeast China.
Korea.4: Rice-farming villages such as Songguk-ri in the southwest grew large and were fortified with palisades and ditches. Bronze daggers and mirrors marked chiefs' status. In the north, Gojoseon's rulers were gaining power and contact with Chinese states across the Liao River.
Korea.5: Iron working began to reach the peninsula from China's Warring States, transforming tools and weapons over the following centuries. Gojoseon grew as a regional power in the north, while the south was home to farming chiefdoms later grouped under the name Jin.
Korea.6: Gojoseon clashed with the Chinese state of Yan, which c. 300 BC pushed it back and seized territory. Korean craftsmen developed the slender bronze dagger style that spread across the peninsula. Iron tools became more common, and southern chiefdoms grew in size and wealth.
Korea.7: Gojoseon remained the leading power in the north while China was unified by the Qin and then the Han. Wars in China sent refugees into the peninsula, bringing iron technology and new ideas. In the south, farming chiefdoms of the Jin area continued to develop.
Korea.8: In 194 BC the refugee leader Wiman seized Gojoseon's throne, and the kingdom grew rich on trade. In 108 BC Han China conquered Gojoseon and set up commanderies, including Lelang near Pyongyang. In the south, the Samhan confederacies of Mahan, Jinhan and Byeonhan took shape.
Korea.9: Tradition dates the founding of Silla to 57 BC, Goguryeo to 37 BC and Baekje to 18 BC, beginning the Three Kingdoms era. In reality these were still small chiefdoms. Buyeo ruled the northern plains, while the Chinese commandery of Lelang spread Chinese culture in the northwest.
Korea.10: Goguryeo grew in the mountains along the Yalu River, raiding Chinese outposts and conquering neighbors. In the south, Samhan chiefdoms formed the seeds of Baekje and Silla, and tradition dates the Gaya confederacy to AD 42. Lelang remained a center of Chinese goods and writing.
Korea.11: Goguryeo became a strong centralized kingdom under King Taejo, expanding its territory. The Gaya states in the south grew wealthy by producing iron and trading it to Japan and Lelang. Baekje and Silla were still building up from local chiefdoms within the Mahan and Jinhan confederacies.
Korea.12: Goguryeo battled Chinese states, and in 244 the Wei general Guanqiu Jian sacked its capital, though the kingdom recovered. Baekje under King Goi consolidated power over the Mahan region. Gaya traded iron with the Wa of Japan, and Silla slowly grew in the southeast.
Korea.13: Goguryeo destroyed the last Chinese commandery, Lelang, in 313, ending Chinese rule in Korea. Buddhism arrived in Goguryeo in 372 and Baekje in 384. Baekje reached a peak under King Geunchogo, and late in the century Goguryeo's King Gwanggaeto began expanding in all directions.
Korea.14: Goguryeo was at its height, with King Gwanggaeto's victories recorded on a great stele in 414. His son Jangsu moved the capital to Pyongyang in 427 and in 475 captured Baekje's capital, forcing Baekje south. Silla was strengthening its monarchy in the southeast.
Korea.15: Silla adopted Buddhism in 527 and expanded under King Jinheung, absorbing the Gaya states by 562 and training elite Hwarang youths. Baekje moved its capital to Sabi in 538 and sent Buddhism to Japan. The three kingdoms fought constantly for control of the Han River valley.
Korea.16: Goguryeo defeated huge Sui Chinese invasions, including at the Salsu River in 612. Silla then allied with Tang China and conquered Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668, unifying Korea. Silla drove out the Tang by 676, and Goguryeo survivors founded Balhae to the north in 698.
Korea.17: Unified Silla enjoyed a golden age of Buddhist art and learning, building Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto at Gyeongju. Society was ruled by a strict 'bone rank' aristocracy. In the north, the kingdom of Balhae flourished, calling itself successor to Goguryeo.
Korea.18: Silla's power declined as aristocrats fought over the throne and provincial lords grew stronger. The merchant Jang Bogo built a maritime trading empire from his base at Cheonghaejin. By 889 peasant revolts spread, and rebels began carving out rival states.
Korea.19: Rebels founded rival kingdoms, and in 918 Wang Geon established the Goryeo dynasty, origin of the name 'Korea'. Silla surrendered in 935 and Goryeo reunited the peninsula in 936, absorbing refugees from Balhae, which fell to the Khitan in 926. Goryeo adopted civil service exams in 958.
Korea.20: Goryeo fought off Khitan invasions, winning a great victory at Gwiju in 1019, and built a long defensive wall in the north. Buddhism thrived, and the first Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks were carved to seek divine protection. An aristocratic civil elite dominated government.
Korea.21: Goryeo celadon pottery reached its peak of beauty, and Kim Busik compiled the Samguk Sagi history in 1145. Tensions between civil and military officials exploded in a military coup in 1170. From 1196 the Choe family ruled as military dictators behind the Goryeo kings.
Korea.22: Goryeo pioneered printing with metal movable type. Mongol invasions began in 1231, and the court fled to Ganghwa Island, carving the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks for protection. In 1259 Goryeo became a Mongol vassal, and its kings married Mongol princesses and supplied ships for the invasions of Japan.
Korea.23: As the Yuan dynasty weakened, King Gongmin restored Goryeo's independence. Red Turban rebels and Japanese pirates ravaged the land. Jikji, printed in 1377, is the oldest surviving book printed with metal type. In 1392 General Yi Seong-gye founded the Joseon dynasty, which embraced Neo-Confucianism.
Korea.24: Joseon ruled from its new capital Hanyang, today's Seoul. King Sejong created the Hangul alphabet in 1443 to help ordinary people read, and sponsored inventions such as rain gauges and water clocks. A national law code organized the Confucian state and its yangban aristocracy.
Korea.25: Bitter factional purges divided Joseon's Confucian scholar-officials, while thinkers such as Yi Hwang and Yi I shaped Korean Neo-Confucianism. Japan's invasions of 1592 to 1598 devastated the country, but Admiral Yi Sun-sin's turtle ships and Ming Chinese aid helped drive the Japanese out.
Korea.26: Joseon was still recovering when the Manchus invaded in 1627 and again in 1636 to 1637, forcing it to become a tributary of the Qing. Korea then limited foreign contact, earning the name 'Hermit Kingdom'. Tax reforms eased burdens on farmers, and commerce slowly grew.
Korea.27: King Yeongjo, who ruled from 1724 to 1776, tried to calm factional fighting with a policy of balanced appointments. Agriculture recovered, markets expanded and the population grew. Scholars of the Silhak, or practical learning, movement began calling for reforms to land, trade and government.
Korea.28: Yeongjo had his own son, Crown Prince Sado, locked in a rice chest to die in 1762. Sado's son King Jeongjo became a reforming ruler who built the Hwaseong fortress at Suwon. Catholicism entered Korea through books from China in 1784, and Silhak scholarship flourished.
Korea.29: After Jeongjo's death, a 1801 persecution killed many Catholics, and powerful in-law families took over the government, ruling through child kings. Corruption and heavy taxes sparked the Hong Gyeong-nae rebellion of 1811 to 1812 in the northwest. Joseon remained closed to the West.
Korea.30: In-law clans kept dominating the Joseon court while peasants suffered from famine and corrupt officials. Catholic converts, along with French missionary priests, were executed in the persecution of 1839. Western ships began appearing off the coasts, seeking trade that Joseon refused.
Korea.31: Choe Je-u founded the Donghak, or Eastern Learning, religion in 1860. The regent Heungseon Daewongun strengthened royal power, persecuted Catholics in 1866 and fought off French and American expeditions in 1866 and 1871, keeping Korea isolated from the outside world.
Korea.32: Japan forced Korea open with the 1876 Ganghwa Treaty, and China, Japan and Russia competed for influence. The Donghak peasant uprising of 1894 triggered the Sino-Japanese War. Japanese agents murdered Queen Min in 1895, and King Gojong proclaimed the Korean Empire in 1897.
Korea.33: After defeating Russia, Japan made Korea a protectorate in 1905. Japan forced Emperor Gojong to abdicate in 1907, and 'righteous armies' fought the Japanese across the countryside. In 1909 Korean patriot An Jung-geun assassinated Itō Hirobumi, Japan's former resident-general in Korea.
Korea.34: Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled through a military government, surveying land and taking much of it for Japanese owners. On March 1, 1919, Koreans rose in nationwide peaceful protests for independence, which were brutally suppressed, and exiles formed a provisional government in Shanghai.
Korea.35: After the March 1st movement, Japan switched to 'cultural rule', allowing some Korean newspapers and groups, though control remained tight. Much of Korea's rice was shipped to Japan while many farmers went hungry. Nationalists and socialists organized, and students protested in Gwangju in 1929.
Korea.36: Japan turned Korea into an industrial and military base for its wars in China. Colonial authorities pushed forced assimilation, requiring Shinto worship, suppressing the Korean language and later pressuring Koreans to take Japanese names. Korean guerrillas fought the Japanese from Manchuria.
Korea.37: During World War II Japan conscripted Koreans as laborers and soldiers and forced many women into military sexual slavery. Korea was liberated in 1945 but divided at the 38th parallel between Soviet and US forces. In 1948 separate states were founded, North Korea and South Korea.
Korea.38: North Korea invaded the South in 1950, and the Korean War drew in US-led UN forces and China, killing about 3 million people before a 1953 armistice with no peace treaty. Afterward, Syngman Rhee ruled the South while Kim Il-sung consolidated total power in the North.
Korea.39: Student protests ousted Syngman Rhee in 1960, but General Park Chung-hee seized power in a 1961 coup and began the South's export-driven 'Miracle on the Han'. South Korea normalized relations with Japan in 1965 and sent troops to Vietnam. North Korea promoted Kim Il-sung's self-reliant Juche ideology.
Korea.40: Park Chung-hee made himself near-dictator under the 1972 Yushin constitution, pushing heavy industries like steel, ships and chemicals. South Korea's economy surged while dissent was repressed. Park was assassinated in 1979. In the North, a personality cult surrounded Kim Il-sung.
Korea.41: General Chun Doo-hwan seized power, and his troops crushed the 1980 Gwangju uprising, killing hundreds. Mass protests won democracy in the South in 1987, and the 1988 Seoul Olympics showcased a modern nation. North Korea grew more isolated and bombed a South Korean airliner in 1987.
Korea.42: Both Koreas joined the UN in 1991. Kim Il-sung died in 1994, and his son Kim Jong-il led North Korea through a devastating famine from 1994 to 1998. South Korea was hit hard by the 1997 Asian financial crisis, and Kim Dae-jung began a 'Sunshine Policy' of engagement with the North.
Korea.43: In 2000 the two Koreas held their first summit, and Kim Dae-jung won the Nobel Peace Prize. South Korea co-hosted the 2002 World Cup and its pop culture spread abroad as the 'Korean Wave'. North Korea conducted its first nuclear test in 2006, deepening tensions.
Korea.44: Kim Jong-un succeeded his father in North Korea in 2011 and expanded its nuclear and missile programs. In the South, President Park Geun-hye was impeached and removed in 2017 over a corruption scandal. Summits in 2018 and 2019 raised hopes of peace, while K-pop and Korean films gained global fame.
Korea.45: North Korea deepened ties with Russia, sending troops to fight in Ukraine's war. In South Korea, President Yoon Suk Yeol's martial-law decree of December 2024 led to his impeachment and removal in 2025, and Lee Jae-myung won the snap election. Han Kang became the first Korean Nobel laureate in literature in 2024.

Oceania / Islanders.0: Humans reached Australia c. 65,000 to 50,000 years ago, crossing open water to the joined landmass of Australia and New Guinea. Aboriginal cultures, among the oldest continuous on Earth, spread across the continent. New Guineans developed some of the world's earliest farming, growing taro and bananas at Kuk swamp c. 7000 BC.
Oceania / Islanders.1: Aboriginal Australians lived in hundreds of distinct language groups, managing the land with fire, trading over long distances and painting rich rock art. In New Guinea's highlands, farmers tended gardens of taro and bananas. The islands beyond the Solomons were still uninhabited, awaiting seafaring settlers.
Oceania / Islanders.2: The dingo arrived in Australia c. 1500 BC, likely brought by seafarers from Southeast Asia. Austronesian voyagers reached the Mariana Islands, and in the Bismarck Archipelago north of New Guinea the Lapita culture appeared, known for finely stamped pottery and skilled ocean sailing.
Oceania / Islanders.3: Lapita voyagers sailed into the open Pacific, reaching Vanuatu and New Caledonia and settling Fiji, Tonga and Samoa c. 1100 to 800 BC, islands no human had touched before. Aboriginal Australians and Papuan-speaking New Guineans continued their long-established ways of life.
Oceania / Islanders.4: In Tonga and Samoa, descendants of the Lapita settlers developed a distinct Ancestral Polynesian culture, language and society. Eastward voyaging paused for many centuries. Across Australia, Aboriginal peoples maintained complex kinship systems, ceremonies and songlines that mapped the land and its stories.
Oceania / Islanders.5: Lapita pottery designs faded into simpler plainware as island communities adapted to local conditions, farming taro, yams and breadfruit and fishing the reefs. Polynesian chiefly society was taking shape in Tonga and Samoa. Aboriginal Australians shaped landscapes through fire-stick farming and seasonal movement.
Oceania / Islanders.6: Pacific islanders lived in chiefdoms based on kinship, gardening and fishing, linked by canoe voyages between neighboring islands. In New Guinea, hundreds of language communities traded shells, stone and pigs. Torres Strait Islanders connected New Guinea and Australia through trade and ceremony.
Oceania / Islanders.7: Micronesian voyagers were spreading through the scattered atolls and high islands of the western Pacific. In western Polynesia, Tonga and Samoa developed chiefdoms with sacred leaders. Aboriginal Australians continued to manage their country, with deep local knowledge of water, plants and seasons.
Oceania / Islanders.8: Seafarers moved into eastern Micronesia, settling islands such as Pohnpei, Kosrae, the Marshalls and Kiribati around this era. In Melanesia, coastal and island peoples developed trade networks in shell valuables, pottery and food. Aboriginal life across Australia remained diverse and resilient.
Oceania / Islanders.9: Across Oceania, peoples lived without states or writing but with rich oral traditions, navigation knowledge and art. Polynesians in Tonga and Samoa still had not sailed farther east. Aboriginal groups in southeastern Australia managed eels with stone channels and traps first built thousands of years earlier.
Oceania / Islanders.10: Western Polynesian societies in Tonga and Samoa grew more stratified, with chiefs claiming descent from the gods. Micronesian communities settled their islands and developed outrigger sailing skills. In Australia, hundreds of Aboriginal nations held their own laws, languages and ceremonies.
Oceania / Islanders.11: Pacific island societies remained centered on chiefs, extended families and gardens, with canoes linking neighboring archipelagos. New Guinea highlanders tended gardens of taro, yams and bananas, long before the sweet potato arrived. Aboriginal Australians traded ochre, stone axes and shells along routes crossing the continent.
Oceania / Islanders.12: Polynesians in the west remained settled for a long pause before further voyaging. In Fiji, populations grew and communities interacted with both Polynesian and Melanesian neighbors. Aboriginal peoples continued to live by hunting, gathering, fishing and careful burning of the land.
Oceania / Islanders.13: Polynesian chiefdoms in Tonga and Samoa held power through sacred status and control of land and food. Older estimates placed settlement of eastern islands like the Marquesas around this time, but newer radiocarbon dating suggests it came much later. Aboriginal Australia remained a mosaic of peoples.
Oceania / Islanders.14: Island communities across Melanesia, Micronesia and western Polynesia continued farming, fishing and voyaging between nearby islands. Navigators kept detailed knowledge of stars, swells and winds. In Australia and New Guinea, life followed deep traditions tied to ancestral lands.
Oceania / Islanders.15: Pacific peoples lived in kin-based communities ruled by chiefs and elders, with ceremonial exchange binding islands together. In Micronesia, communities on Yap, Palau and the Carolines built ties through voyaging. Aboriginal Australians maintained their law, art and land management across the continent.
Oceania / Islanders.16: Polynesian, Melanesian and Micronesian societies continued to grow and diversify, with chiefs organizing food production and feasting. In northern Australia and New Guinea, coastal peoples traded across the Torres Strait. Eastern Polynesia beyond Samoa still remained unsettled.
Oceania / Islanders.17: Western Polynesian societies were developing more powerful chiefdoms, and voyaging skills were preparing them for a great expansion east. Across Melanesia, communities built trade and marriage networks. Aboriginal Australians maintained their long-established ways of living with the land.
Oceania / Islanders.18: After many centuries in Tonga and Samoa, Polynesians had refined their double-hulled canoes and navigation, yet the vast eastern Pacific remained empty of people. In Fiji and across Melanesia, island communities traded and intermarried, and Aboriginal Australians continued to care for their country through ceremony, law and fire.
Oceania / Islanders.19: In the Mariana Islands, the Chamorro latte period began c. 900, when people raised houses on large stone pillars. Polynesians in Tonga and Samoa were preparing for a wave of long-distance voyages, and tradition dates the founding of the sacred Tu'i Tonga line to about this period.
Oceania / Islanders.20: Polynesian voyagers launched a remarkable eastward expansion, settling the Society Islands, Cook Islands and Marquesas, then Hawaii and Rapa Nui (Easter Island) c. 1000 to 1200. They carried crops, pigs, chickens and dogs in large double-hulled canoes, navigating by stars and swells.
Oceania / Islanders.21: On Pohnpei, the Saudeleur dynasty built the stone city of Nan Madol on artificial islets, ruling the island. Polynesian settlement of Rapa Nui and other far islands continued, and Tonga's Tu'i Tonga chiefs extended their influence. Aboriginal peoples continued their ancient ways across Australia.
Oceania / Islanders.22: Māori ancestors settled New Zealand c. 1250 to 1300, the last major landmass reached by humans, and hunted the giant flightless moa. Rapa Nui islanders began carving their famous moai statues. Tonga's chiefs built a maritime network across the region, and Hawaiian chiefdoms grew.
Oceania / Islanders.23: In New Zealand, Māori hunting drove the moa toward extinction by c. 1400, and communities shifted to gardening and fishing. Long-distance voyaging across Polynesia gradually declined, leaving island groups more isolated. Rapa Nui islanders continued raising moai, and Hawaiian chiefdoms grew larger.
Oceania / Islanders.24: Māori society shifted toward tribal groups (iwi) living in fortified hilltop villages called pā, as conflicts over land grew. Hawaiian chiefs ruled larger territories with complex irrigation and fishponds. Moriori settled the Chatham Islands, and Rapa Nui islanders still carved moai.
Oceania / Islanders.25: Magellan crossed the Pacific in 1521 and reached Guam, the first European contact with Pacific islanders. Spanish voyages later reached the Solomon Islands. Otherwise, Polynesian, Melanesian and Micronesian societies continued under their own chiefs, and Aboriginal Australia remained unknown to Europeans.
Oceania / Islanders.26: Dutch sailors reached northern Australia in 1606, and Abel Tasman reached Tasmania and New Zealand in 1642, clashing with Māori. Spain colonized Guam and the Marianas from 1668, and war and disease devastated the Chamorro people. On Pohnpei, the Saudeleur dynasty was overthrown.
Oceania / Islanders.27: Dutch explorer Jacob Roggeveen reached Rapa Nui in 1722 and passed Samoa. Makassan fishermen from Sulawesi began visiting northern Australia to gather sea cucumbers, trading with Yolngu people. Elsewhere, Pacific islanders and Aboriginal Australians lived largely untouched by Europeans.
Oceania / Islanders.28: Europeans arrived in force. Captain Cook's voyages of 1768 to 1779 charted New Zealand, eastern Australia and Hawaii. In 1788 the British First Fleet founded a penal colony at Sydney, and smallpox and violence soon devastated local Aboriginal people. Kamehameha was rising to power in Hawaii.
Oceania / Islanders.29: Kamehameha unified the Hawaiian Islands by 1810. In New Zealand, Māori tribes armed with muskets fought devastating intertribal wars. British settlement spread to Tasmania and across the Blue Mountains, and missionaries converted rulers in Tahiti and, after 1820, in Hawaii.
Oceania / Islanders.30: Britain expanded its colonies in Australia, founding Perth, Melbourne and Adelaide, and frontier wars nearly destroyed Tasmania's Aboriginal people. In 1840 Māori chiefs and the British signed the Treaty of Waitangi in New Zealand, though its meaning was disputed. France took control of Tahiti in 1842.
Oceania / Islanders.31: Australian gold rushes from 1851 drew huge immigration and made colonies rich and self-governing. Wars between Māori and colonial forces raged in New Zealand in the 1860s, leading to land confiscations. Labor recruiters known as blackbirders took Pacific islanders to Queensland, and Fiji became a British colony in 1874.
Oceania / Islanders.32: New Zealand in 1893 became the first nation to give women the vote. In Hawaii, American businessmen overthrew the monarchy in 1893 and the US annexed the islands in 1898. Germany and Britain split eastern New Guinea, Chile annexed Rapa Nui in 1888, and Indian laborers arrived in Fiji.
Oceania / Islanders.33: Australia federated in 1901 as a dominion and quickly adopted the 'White Australia' immigration policy. New Zealand became a dominion in 1907. Europeans and Americans now controlled nearly every Pacific island, while Aboriginal Australians faced restrictive laws and removal of children.
Oceania / Islanders.34: In World War I, Australian and New Zealand troops fought at Gallipoli in 1915, forging the ANZAC identity. Australia seized German New Guinea, New Zealand took Samoa and Japan took Micronesia. The 1918 influenza pandemic killed about a fifth of Western Samoa's people.
Oceania / Islanders.35: Former German islands became League of Nations mandates run by Australia, New Zealand and Japan. In Samoa, the Mau movement campaigned peacefully for self-rule. Australia's parliament moved to Canberra in 1927, while the 1928 Coniston massacre showed continuing frontier violence against Aboriginal people.
Oceania / Islanders.36: The Great Depression hit export-dependent Australia and New Zealand hard. New Zealand police killed Mau leader Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III in 1929, but the movement continued. Aboriginal activists held a Day of Mourning in 1938, and Japan fortified its Micronesian islands.
Oceania / Islanders.37: The Pacific War of 1941 to 1945 brought battles at Midway, Guadalcanal, Kokoda and across the islands, and Japan bombed Darwin in 1942. In 1946 US nuclear tests began at Bikini Atoll in the Marshall Islands. Postwar Australia launched mass immigration from Europe.
Oceania / Islanders.38: Australia, New Zealand and the US signed the ANZUS alliance in 1951. US hydrogen bomb tests contaminated Marshall Islanders, and Britain tested atomic weapons in Australia at Maralinga. Melbourne hosted the 1956 Olympics as Australia's economy and population grew.
Oceania / Islanders.39: Western Samoa became the first independent Pacific island nation in 1962, followed by Nauru in 1968. In 1967 Australians voted overwhelmingly to count Aboriginal people in the census and allow federal laws for them. France began nuclear tests in French Polynesia, and both ANZAC nations sent troops to Vietnam.
Oceania / Islanders.40: Pacific island nations won independence, including Fiji and Tonga in 1970, Papua New Guinea in 1975 and the Solomons, Tuvalu and Kiribati by 1979. Australia ended the White Australia policy, Aboriginal activists set up a Tent Embassy, and New Zealand created the Waitangi Tribunal in 1975.
Oceania / Islanders.41: Vanuatu gained independence in 1980, and the Marshall Islands and Micronesia entered free association with the US. Fiji suffered two military coups in 1987. French agents sank the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland in 1985, and New Zealand declared itself nuclear-free.
Oceania / Islanders.42: Australia's High Court recognized Aboriginal native title in the 1992 Mabo decision. New Zealand began major treaty settlements with Māori iwi. France ended Pacific nuclear tests in 1996, Bougainville's civil war ended with a 1998 truce, and Australia led peacekeepers into East Timor in 1999.
Oceania / Islanders.43: Sydney hosted the 2000 Olympics. Fiji saw further coups in 2000 and 2006, and an Australian-led mission restored order in the Solomon Islands from 2003. In 2008 Australia formally apologized to the Stolen Generations of Aboriginal children taken from their families.
Oceania / Islanders.44: Earthquakes devastated Christchurch in 2010 to 2011, and a terrorist killed 51 worshippers at two Christchurch mosques in 2019. Bougainville voted overwhelmingly for independence from Papua New Guinea in 2019. Pacific nations warned of climate change as China competed with Australia for regional influence.
Oceania / Islanders.45: Rising seas threaten atoll nations like Tuvalu and Kiribati, and Australia offered Tuvaluans a migration pathway in 2023. Tonga's 2022 volcanic eruption was the largest in decades. Australians rejected an Indigenous Voice to Parliament in 2023, and a Vanuatu-led campaign won a 2025 world court opinion on climate duties.
